Main article: [Ravens–Steelers rivalry](/wiki/Ravens%E2%80%93Steelers_rivalry "Ravens–Steelers rivalry")

Pittsburgh's rivalry with the [Baltimore Ravens](/wiki/Baltimore_Ravens "Baltimore Ravens") has had several memorable matchups and has escalated into a fierce competitive sports rivalry. The rivalry features the league's two longest tenure coaches Mike Tomlin and Raven's coach [John Harbaugh](/wiki/John_Harbaugh "John Harbaugh"). Both teams handed the other their first losses at their current home stadiums. The Steelers won the inaugural game played at [Baltimore's](/wiki/Baltimore,_Maryland "Baltimore, Maryland") [M&T Bank Stadium](/wiki/M%26T_Bank_Stadium "M&T Bank Stadium") in [1998](/wiki/1998_NFL_season "1998 NFL season"), 20–13, and three years later the [Ravens](/wiki/Baltimore_Ravens "Baltimore Ravens") handed the Steelers their first-ever loss at [Heinz Field](/wiki/Heinz_Field "Heinz Field"), 13–10. Later that season ([2001](/wiki/2001_NFL_season "2001 NFL season")) Pittsburgh won a [divisional playoff game](/wiki/2001%E2%80%9302_NFL_playoffs#AFC:_Pittsburgh_Steelers_27,_Baltimore_Ravens_10 "2001–02 NFL playoffs") 27–10 against Baltimore, who was the [defending Super Bowl champion](/wiki/Super_Bowl_XXXV "Super Bowl XXXV"). During their NFL championship season in [2000](/wiki/2000_Baltimore_Ravens_season "2000 Baltimore Ravens season"), the Ravens defeated the Steelers [in Pittsburgh](/wiki/Three_Rivers_Stadium "Three Rivers Stadium"), 16–0, in the season opener with the Steelers later exacting revenge, 9–6, in Baltimore (the Ravens' final loss of the season). During the Steelers 2008 Championship run, they beat the Ravens three times, including a win in the AFC Championship game. The two teams complement each other by consistently fielding strong defenses. The Steelers lead the all-time series (including playoffs), 32–24.[[111]](#cite_note-112) The teams have met four times in the postseason, with the Steelers owning a 3–1 record.[[112]](#cite_note-j269-113)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/58/Vegetation_Africa.png/330px-Vegetation_Africa.png)](/wiki/File:Vegetation_Africa.png)

The main biomes in Africa

Africa has over 3,000 [protected areas](/wiki/Protected_area "Protected area"), with 198 marine protected areas, 50 biosphere reserves, and 80 wetlands reserves. Significant habitat destruction, increases in human population and poaching are reducing Africa's biological diversity and [arable land](/wiki/Arable_land "Arable land"). Human encroachment, civil unrest and the introduction of non-native species threaten biodiversity in Africa. This has been exacerbated by administrative problems, inadequate personnel and funding problems.[[160]](#cite_note-environmentalatlas-168)

[Deforestation](/wiki/Deforestation "Deforestation") is affecting Africa at twice the world rate, according to the United Nations Environment Programme ([UNEP](/wiki/UNEP "UNEP")).[[168]](#cite_note-176) The deforestation rate of 4.08 million hectares in 2000–2015 declined to 3.45 million ha per year in 2015–2025.[[169]](#cite_note-177) According to the University of Pennsylvania African Studies Center, 31% of Africa's pasture lands and 19% of its forests and woodlands are classified as degraded, and Africa is losing over four million hectares of forest per year, which is twice the average deforestation rate for the rest of the world.[[160]](#cite_note-environmentalatlas-168) Some sources claim that approximately 90% of the original, virgin forests in West Africa have been destroyed.[[170]](#cite_note-178) Over 90% of [Madagascar](/wiki/Madagascar "Madagascar")'s original forests have been destroyed since the arrival of humans 2000 years ago.[[171]](#cite_note-179) About 65% of Africa's agricultural land suffers from [soil degradation](/wiki/Soil_degradation "Soil degradation").[[172]](#cite_note-180)

The *Oxford Olympics Study 2016* estimates the outturn cost of the Sydney 2000 Summer Olympics at US$5 billion in 2015 dollars and cost overrun at 90% in real terms.[[9]](#cite_note-10) This includes sports-related costs only; that is, (i) *operational costs* incurred by the organising committee to stage the Games, e.g., expenditures for technology, transportation, workforce, administration, security, catering, ceremonies, and medical services, and (ii) *direct capital costs* incurred by the host city and country or private investors to build; e.g., the competition venues, the Olympic village, international broadcast centre, and media and press centre, which are required to host the Games. Indirect capital costs are *not* included, such as for road, [rail](/wiki/Olympic_Park_railway_line,_Sydney "Olympic Park railway line, Sydney"), airport infrastructure, hotel upgrades, or other business investments incurred in preparation for the Games but not directly related to staging the Games. The cost for Sydney 2000 compares with a cost of US$4.6 billion for Rio 2016, US$40‍–‍44 billion for Beijing 2008, and US$51 billion for Sochi 2014, the most expensive Olympics in history. The average cost for the Summer Games since 1960 is US$5.2 billion, average cost overrun is 176%.

In 2000, the [Auditor-General of New South Wales](/wiki/Auditor-General_of_New_South_Wales "Auditor-General of New South Wales") reported that the Sydney Games cost [A$](/wiki/A$ "A$")6.6 billion, with a net cost to the public between A$1.7 and A$2.4 billion.[[10]](#cite_note-11)[[11]](#cite_note-12) In the years leading up to the Games, funds were shifted from education and health programs to cover Olympic expenses.[[12]](#cite_note-FindlingPelle2004-13)

Lena Dunham's 2010 second feature, *[Tiny Furniture](/wiki/Tiny_Furniture "Tiny Furniture")*—which she wrote, directed and starred in—received positive reviews at festivals as well as awards attention, including Best Narrative Feature at [South by Southwest](/wiki/South_by_Southwest "South by Southwest") and Best First Screenplay at the 2010 [Independent Spirit Awards](/wiki/Independent_Spirit_Awards "Independent Spirit Awards").[[49]](#cite_note-slate1-49)[[50]](#cite_note-tvblend1-50) The independent film's success earned her the opportunity to collaborate with [Judd Apatow](/wiki/Judd_Apatow "Judd Apatow") for an [HBO](/wiki/HBO "HBO") pilot.[[51]](#cite_note-51) Judd Apatow said he was drawn to Dunham's imagination after watching *Tiny Furniture*, and added that *Girls* would provide men with an insight into "realistic females."[[1]](#cite_note-tca-1)

Some of the struggles facing Dunham's character Hannah—including being cut off financially from her parents, becoming a writer and making unfortunate decisions—are inspired by Dunham's real-life experiences.[[1]](#cite_note-tca-1) The show's look is achieved by furnishings at a number of vintage boutiques in New York, including [Brooklyn Flea](/wiki/Brooklyn_Flea "Brooklyn Flea") and [Geminola](/wiki/Geminola "Geminola") owned by [Jemima Kirke](/wiki/Jemima_Kirke "Jemima Kirke")'s mother.[[52]](#cite_note-52)

**Tomas Gösta Tranströmer** (Swedish: [[ˈtʊ̌mːas ˈjœ̂sːta ˈtrâːnˌstrœmːɛr]](/wiki/Help:IPA/Swedish "Help:IPA/Swedish"); 15 April 1931 – 26 March 2015) was a Swedish poet, psychologist and translator.[[1]](#cite_note-1) His poems captured the long winters in [Sweden](/wiki/Sweden "Sweden"), the rhythm of the seasons and the palpable, atmospheric beauty of nature.[[2]](#cite_note-nyt-2) Tranströmer's work is also characterized by a sense of mystery and wonder underlying the routine of everyday life, a quality which often gives his poems a religious dimension.[[3]](#cite_note-PE-3) He has been described as a [Christian](/wiki/Christians "Christians") poet.[[4]](#cite_note-CPR-4)

Tranströmer is acclaimed as one of the most important Scandinavian writers since the [Second World War](/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"). Critics praised his poetry for its accessibility, even in translation.[[2]](#cite_note-nyt-2) His poetry has been translated into over 60 languages.[[2]](#cite_note-nyt-2) He received many awards for his poetry, including the [2011 Nobel Prize in Literature](/wiki/2011_Nobel_Prize_in_Literature "2011 Nobel Prize in Literature").[[5]](#cite_note-ap_nobel-5)
